claims.text: On ordinary 64-bit Intel/AMD Windows, the 32-bit compatibility subsystem switches the processor between modes rather than emulating instructions, which is computationally cheap, and Microsoft says performance is similar to native 32-bit Windows. So the per-call cost of a 32-bit compiler there is mostly not instruction translation, and the large overhead appears when software emulation is involved (non-x64 hosts) or comes from the surrounding work each launch does.

claims.text: Compatibility layers add work on every launch beyond code execution: redirecting system-folder and registry access for 32-bit programs, loading Wine-style DLL sets, and for Wine the choice between built-in and native DLLs. These costs sit in the loader and file/registry paths, so they can in principle be reduced by caching, keeping the process resident or trimming what loads, without touching the machine code the compiler emits. The sources describe these mechanisms but give no per-call timings, so how much each contributes is unknown.

claims.text: Incremental compilers reuse earlier output and recompile only changed pieces, which limits how much optimization they can apply because they see only a narrow slice of the program. The common practice is therefore to use incremental builds during development and a standard full batch compiler for release, so what you ship is not shaped by leftover state from earlier compilations.

claims.text: A long-lived Java runtime compiles code on the fly based on what it observes the program doing, and keeps the results in memory so later calls skip the slow path. As a result, what gets compiled and how fast it runs depends on the workload history so far, and thousands of methods compiled at startup measurably affect startup time. Measurements taken early or on a differently exercised process will not match steady-state behavior.
